'''apparence†, apparency†''' (a-pãr′ens, -ẹn-si), ''n.'' [ME. ''apparence, apparens, aparence, -aunce,'' also ''apparencie,'' < OF. ''aparence, aparance,'' F. ''apparence'' = Pr. ''apparencia, aparensa'' = Sp. ''apariencia'' = Pg. ''apparencia'' = It. ''apparenza,'' < L. ''apparentia,'' appearance, in ML. also simulation, < ''apparen(t-)s,'' apparent: see ''apparent.'' Cf. ''appearance.''] '''1.''' Preparation; making ready. —'''2.''' Superficial seeming; external semblance; appearance: as, “vain and gaudy ''apparencies,''” ''Bp. Wren.''
{{smaller block|Outward ''apparance'' is no authentic instance of the inward desires.
{{right|''Middleton,'' Family of Love, i. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' The quality of being apparent to the senses or to the mind; apparentness.—'''4.''' The position of being an heir apparent. ''N. E. D.''

'''apparent''' (a-pãr′ent), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''apparant, -aunt, aparant,'' also by apheresis ''parent,'' < OF. ''aparant, -ent,'' F. ''apparent'' = Pr. ''apparent'' = Sp. ''aparente'' = Pg. It. ''apparente,'' < L. ''apparen(t-)s,'' ppr. of ''apparēre, adparēre,'' come in sight, appear: see ''appear'' and ''-ant''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Exposed to the sense of sight; open to view; capable of being seen, or easily seen; visible to the eye; within the range of vision.
{{smaller block|<poem>By some ''apparent'' sign
Let us have knowledge at the court of guard.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' 1 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}
As we rapidly approached the land the beauty of the scenery became more fully ''apparent.''
{{right|''Lady Brassey,'' Voyage of Sunbeam, I. ii.}}}}

'''II.'''† ''n.'' An heir apparent.
{{smaller block|<poem>''K. Hen.'' Draw thy sword in right. . . .
''Prince.'' I’ll draw it as ''apparent'' to the crown,
And in that quarrel use it to the death.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 2.}}}}

'''apparently''' (a-pãr′ent-li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' Openly; evidently to the senses or the intellect.
{{smaller block|<poem>I would not spare my brother in this case,
If he should scorn me so ''apparently''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Seemingly; in appearance, whether in reality or not; as far as one can judge: as, he is ''apparently'' well; only ''apparently'' friendly.
{{smaller block|The motions of a watch, ''apparently'' uncaused by anything external, seem spontaneous.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 65.}}}}

'''apparentness''' (a-pãr′ent-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being apparent; plainness to the eye or to the mind; visibleness; obviousness.

'''appeach†''' (a-pēch′), ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. also ''apeach'', < ME. ''appechen'', ''apechen'' (and by apheresis ''pechen'', > mod. E. {{smaller block|He did, amongst many others, ''appeach'' Sir William Stanley, the lord chamberlain. {{right|''Bacon'', Hen. VII.}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|apparatus|269|appeachment}}</noinclude>ments, utensils, appliances, or materials intended, adapted, and necessary for the accomplishment of some purpose, such as mechanical work, experimenting, etc.: as, chemical, philosophical, or surgical ''apparatus.''

{{smaller block|The whole military ''apparatus'' of the archduke was put in motion.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 17.}}}}

{{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In ''physiol.'', a collection of organs which, though differing in structure, all minister to the same function: as, the respiratory ''apparatus''; the digestive ''apparatus.'' (''b'') A collection of materials for any literary work: as, critical ''apparatus'' for the study of the Greek text of the New Testament.—'''Apparatus belli''' (Latin), materials of war; ammunition; military stores.—'''Apparatus Sculptoris''' (New Latin), the Sculptor’s Workshop, a constellation situated in that region of the heavens which lies immediately to the east of the large star Fomalhaut, or α Piscis Australis. It barely rises above the horizon in the northern hemisphere.}}

'''apparel''' (a̤-par′el), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''appareled'' or ''apparelled'', ppr. ''appareling'' or ''apparelling.''   [Early mod. E. also ''aparel'', ''aparrell'', etc., < ME. ''aparailen'', ''apparailen'', ''-aylen'', ''-eilen'', ''-eylen'', etc., and by apheresis ''parailen'', < OF. ''aparailler'', ''apareiller'', F. ''appareiller'', dress, prepare, = Pr. ''aparelhar'' = Sp. ''aparejar'' = Pg. ''apparelhar'' = It. ''apparecchiare'', < L. as if *''adpariculare'', make equal or fit, < ''ad'', to, + *''pariculus'' (> It. ''parecchio'' = Pg. ''parelho'' = Sp. ''parejo'' = Pr. ''parelh'' = F. ''pareil'', equal, like), dim. of ''par'', equal: see ''par.'']   '''1†.''' To make ready; prepare; fit out; put in proper order.

{{smaller block|For ther he wolde hire weddying ''apparaile.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 2473.}}}}

'''2.''' To dress or clothe; adorn or set off; deck with ornaments.

{{smaller block|Behold, they which are gorgeously ''apparelled'', and live delicately, are in kings’ courts. {{right|Luke vii. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is no greater charity to clothe his body, than ''apparel'' the nakedness of his soul.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|She did ''apparel'' her apparel, and with the preciousness of her body made it most sumptuous. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}
{{smaller block|You may have trees ''apparelled'' with flowers by boring holes in them, putting into them earth, and setting seeds of violets. {{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 504.}}}}
'''3.''' To furnish with external apparatus; equip: as, ships ''appareled'' for sea.

'''apparel''' (a̤-par′el), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''aparel'', ''aparrel'', etc., and ''parel'', ''parrell'', etc., < ME. ''aparel'', ''apparail'', ''apareil'', and by apheresis ''parel'', < OF. ''aparail'', ''apareil'', ''aparel'', preparation, equipment, F. ''appareil'', preparation, provision, = Pr. ''aparelh'' = Sp. ''aparejo'' = Pg. ''apparelho'' = It. ''apparecchio''; from the verb.]   '''1†.''' Preparation; the work of preparing or providing.—'''2.''' Things prepared or provided; articles or materials to be used for a given purpose; apparatus; equipment. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a''†) The furniture, appendages, or attachments of a house. (''b'') ''Naut.'', the furnishings or equipment of a ship, as sails, rigging, anchors, guns, etc.}}
{{smaller block|The carpenters were building their magazines of oares, masts, &c., for an hundred gallys and ships, which have all their ''aparell'' and furniture neere them.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, June, 1645.}}}}
'''3.''' A person’s outer clothing or vesture; raiment; external array; hence, figuratively, aspect; guise. {{smaller block|<poem>Costly thy habit as thy purse can buy,
But not express’d in fancy; rich, not gaudy:
For the ''apparel'' oft proclaims the man.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|At publick devotion his resigned carriage made religion appear in the natural ''apparel'' of simplicity. {{right|''Tatler.''}}}}
'''4.''' ''Eccles.'', an ornament of the alb and amice, found as a simple fringe or colored stripe earlier {{img float|file=century v01 p0295 c1f1.png|width=157px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Part of the Apparel of the Alb of Becket, in the cathedral of Sens, France. (From Viollet-le-Duc’s “Dict. du Mobilier français.”)}}}} than the tenth century, most extensively employed and elaborate in workmanship during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and still used in the form of pieces of lace sewed upon silk. {{smaller|The apparels of the alb are either oblong quadrangular patches on the wrists and on the skirt before and behind, or bands completely encircling the skirt and wrists. The apparel of the amice is on the outside part, which is turned down like a collar. It was often in orphrey-work adorned with precious stones so disposed as to form sacred emblems.}} ='''Syn. 3.''' Raiment, costume, attire, clothes, garb, habiliments.

'''apparelment†''', ''n.''   [< ME. ''apparaillement'', ''aparaylment'', < OF. ''apareillement'' = Pr. ''aparelhamen'', ''aparellamen'' = OSp. ''aparejamiento'' = Pg. ''apparelhamento'' = It. ''apparecchiamento'': see ''apparel'' and ''-ment.'']   Equipment; clothing; adornment.   ''Chaucer'', Boëthius.

'''apparence†, apparency†''' (a-pãr′ens, -ẹn-si), ''n.''   [ME. ''apparence, apparens, aparence, -aunce,'' also ''apparencie,'' < OF. ''aparence, aparance,'' F. ''apparence'' = Pr. ''apparencia, aparensa'' = Sp. ''apariencia'' = Pg. ''apparencia'' = It. ''apparenza,'' < L. ''apparentia,'' appearance, in ML. also simulation, < ''apparen(t-)s,'' apparent: see ''apparent.'' Cf. ''appearance.'']   '''1.''' Preparation; making ready. —'''2.''' Superficial seeming; external semblance; appearance: as, “vain and gaudy ''apparencies,''” ''Bp. Wren.''
{{smaller block|Outward ''apparance'' is no authentic instance of the inward desires.
{{right|''Middleton,'' Family of Love, i. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' The quality of being apparent to the senses or to the mind; apparentness.—'''4.''' The position of being an heir apparent.   ''N. E. D.''

'''apparent''' (a-pãr′ent), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''apparant, -aunt, aparant,'' also by apheresis ''parent,'' < OF. ''aparant, -ent,'' F. ''apparent'' = Pr. ''apparent'' = Sp. ''aparente'' = Pg. It. ''apparente,'' < L. ''apparen(t-)s,'' ppr. of ''apparēre, adparēre,'' come in sight, appear: see ''appear'' and ''-ant''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Exposed to the sense of sight; open to view; capable of being seen, or easily seen; visible to the eye; within the range of vision.
{{smaller block|<poem>By some ''apparent'' sign
Let us have knowledge at the court of guard.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' 1 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|As we rapidly approached the land the beauty of the scenery became more fully ''apparent.''
{{right|''Lady Brassey,'' Voyage of Sunbeam, I. ii.}}}}

'''2.''' Capable of being clearly perceived or understood; obvious; plain or clear; evident: as, the wisdom of the Creator is ''apparent'' in his works.
{{smaller block|At that time Cicero had vehement suspicions of Cæsar, but no ''apparent'' proof to convince him. {{right|''North.''}}}}
'''3.''' Having the character of a mere seeming or appearance, in distinction from what is true or real: as, the ''apparent'' motion of the sun; his anger was only ''apparent.''
{{smaller block|For the powers of nature, notwithstanding their ''apparent'' magnitude, are limited and stationary.
{{right|''Buckle'', Civilization, I. 46.}}}}
{{smaller block|Culture inverts the vulgar view of nature, and brings the mind to call that ''apparent'' which it uses to call real, and that real which it uses to call visionary. {{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}}
'''4†.''' Probable; likely: as, “the three ''apparent'' candidates,” ''H. Walpole.''—{{smaller|'''Apparent day,''' the real or true solar day, as distinguished from the ''mean day.'' See ''day.''—'''Apparent declination,''' the declination of the apparent place of a star.—'''Apparent diameter of a heavenly body,''' the angle which its diameter subtends at the eye, that is, the angle made by lines drawn from the extremities of its diameter to the eye.—'''Apparent double point,''' in ''math.'', a point on a curve in space which appears to be double to an eye placed at a given point.—'''Apparent easement.''' See ''easement.''—'''Apparent''' or '''intentional ens.''' See ''ens.''—'''Apparent figure,''' the figure or shape under which an object appears when seen at a distance.—'''Apparent horizon.''' Same as ''visible horizon'' (which see, under ''horizon'').—'''Apparent magnitude.''' See ''magnitude.''—'''Apparent noon,''' the instant at which the center of the sun crosses the meridian.—'''Apparent place of a star,''' etc., the place on the celestial sphere where it would appear but for refraction; sometimes the place where it does appear.—'''Apparent position,''' in ''optics'', the position in which an object appears to be when seen through glass, water, or any other diffracting medium, as distinguished from its true position. See ''refraction''.—'''Apparent right ascension''', the right ascension of the apparent place of a star.—'''Apparent time''', the hour-angle of the sun.—'''Heir apparent.''' See ''heir''. ='''Syn. 1''' and '''2.''' Clear, distinct, manifest, patent, unmistakable.—'''3.''' Ostensible.}}

'''II.'''† ''n.'' An heir apparent.

''Prince.'' I’ll draw it as ''apparent'' to the crown,

{{smaller block|The motions of a watch, ''apparently'' uncaused by anything external, seem spontaneous.

'''apparish†''' (a-par′ish), ''v. t.''   [Late ME. ''apparysshe'', < OF. ''apariss-'', stem of certain parts of ''aparir'', ''aparer'', < L. ''apparēre'', appear: see ''appear''.]   To appear.   ''Caxton'', Golden Legend. (''N. E. D.'')

'''apparition''' (ap-a-rish′ọn), ''n.''   [< F. ''apparition'', < ML. ''apparitio(n-)'', an appearance, epiphany, also attendants, L. only in sense of attendance, attendants, < ''apparēre'', ''adparēre'', pp. ''apparitus'', {{smaller|''adparitus'', appear, attend, wait upon, serve: see ''appear'', ''apparent'', and ''apparitor''.]}} '''1.''' The act of appearing or coming into sight; appearance; the state of being visible; visibility.
{{smaller block|<poem>When the holy churchman join’d our hands,
Our vows were real then; the ceremony
Was not in ''apparition'', but in act.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The sudden ''apparition'' of the Spaniards. {{right|''Prescott.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Louis XIV. appeared [at Chambord] on several occasions, and the ''apparition'' was characteristically brilliant.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 39.}}}}
'''2.''' That which appears or becomes visible; an appearance, especially of a remarkable or phenomenal kind.
{{smaller block|Let us interrogate the great ''apparition'' that shines so peacefully around us. {{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}}
{{smaller block|Miss Edgeworth taught a contempt of falsehood, no less in its most graceful than in its meanest ''apparitions.''
{{right|''Marg. Fuller'', Woman in 19th Cent., p. 131.}}}}
Specifically—'''3.''' A ghostly appearance; a specter or phantom: now the usual sense of the word.
{{smaller block|Tender minds should not receive early impressions of goblins, spectres, ''apparitions'', wherewith maids fright them into compliance. {{right|''Locke.''}}}}
'''4.''' In ''astron.'', the first appearance of a star or other luminary after having been obscured: opposed to ''occultation''.—{{smaller|'''Circle of apparition,''' or '''of perpetual apparition,''' the bounding circle of that part of the heavens which is always visible; that circle}} of declination which is tangent to the horizon. ='''Syn. 3.''' ''Specter, Phantom'', etc. See ''ghost''.

'''apparitional''' (ap-a̤-rish′on-a̤l), ''a.''   [< ''apparition'' + ''-al''.]   '''1.''' Resembling an apparition; having the nature of a phantom; spectral.—'''2.''' Capable of appearing; endowed with materializing qualities.—{{smaller|'''Apparitional soul''', a thin, unsubstantial human image conceived, in certain phases of primitive thought, as the cause of life and mind, capable of quitting the body for a time or altogether, and so leaving it insensible or dead, and when thus absent from it appearing to other individuals asleep or awake.}}
{{smaller block|Closely allied . . . to the primitive notion of the ''apparitional soul'', is the belief in the soul’s existence after death.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', II. 55.}}}}
{{smaller block|That the ''apparitional'' human ''soul'' bears the likeness of its fleshly body, is the principle implicitly accepted by all who believe it really and objectively present in dream or vision.
{{right|''E. B. Tylor'', Prim. Culture, I. 406.}}}}

'''apparitor''' (a-par′i-tor), ''n.''   [L., a servant, esp. a public servant (lictor, scribe, military aide, priest, etc.), < ''apparēre, adparēre'', attend, serve: see ''apparition''.]   '''1.''' In ''Rom. antiq.'', any officer who attended magistrates and judges to execute their orders.—'''2.''' Any officer of a civil court, or his servant or attendant.—'''3.''' Any one who puts in an appearance; an appearer. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The Higher Court . . . in which . . . every Human Soul is an ''apparitor''.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Past and Present, p. 211.}}}}
'''4.''' ''Eccles.'', a messenger or an officer who serves the process of a spiritual court; the lowest officer of an ecclesiastical tribunal.
{{smaller block|He swallowed all the Roman hierarchy, from the pope to the ''apparitor''.
{{right|''Ayliffe'', Parergon.}}}}

{{smaller block|When my great-grandfather wished to read the Bible to his family, . . . one of the children stood at the door to give notice if he saw the ''apparitor'' coming, who was an officer of the spiritual court. {{right|''Franklin'', Autobiog., pp. 8, 9.}}}}
'''5.''' The beadle in a university, who carries the mace.

'''appaumée''' (a-pō-mā′), ''a.''   [F., < ''à'' (< L. ''ad'', to) + ''paume'', the palm of the hand: see ''palm''.]   In ''her.'', open and extended so as to show the palm with thumb and fingers at full length: said of the human hand. Also spelled ''apaumée.'' {{img float|file=century v01 p0295 c3f1.png|width=60px|align=right|cap={{smaller|A Right Hand Appaumée.}}}}

'''appay†''', ''v. t.'' See ''apay''.

'''appeach†''' (a-pēch′), ''v. t.''   [Early mod. E. also ''apeach'', < ME. ''appechen'', ''apechen'' (and by apheresis ''pechen'', > mod. E. ''peach''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.), reduced from earlier ''empechen'', whence the usual mod. form ''impeach'', q. v. Cf. ''appair'', ''impair''.]   '''1.''' To impeach.
{{smaller block|He did, amongst many others, ''appeach'' Sir William Stanley, the lord chamberlain. {{right|''Bacon'', Hen. VII.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor can’st, nor dar’st thou, traitor, on the plain

{{smaller block|<poem>And oft of error did himselfe ''appeach''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xi. 40.}}}}

'''appeacher†''' (a-pē′chėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''apechowre'' (Prompt. Parv.), < AF. ''enpechour'', OF. ''empecheor'': see ''appeach'' and ''-er''.]   An accuser.

'''appeachment†''' (a-pēch′ment), ''n.''   [< ''appeach'' + ''-ment''. Cf. ''impeachment''.]   Accusation; impeachment; charge.
{{smaller block|The duke’s answers to his ''appeachments'', in number thirteen, I find very diligently and civilly couched.
{{right|''Sir H. Wotton.''}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
